# Is the nearest blue-uniformed man safe if he stays still?

**Short answer: Yes. He is safe where he stands. The train will pass in front of
him (between him and the viewer) and run out of the picture at the bottom-right,
several metres clear of him.**

## Which man the question is about

The painting shows several figures in blue. In the middle distance, near the
parked cars and the yellow van, there are two or three blue-clad dockers/sailors
(around the middle of the picture, roughly at the level of the car roofs). Those
are all further away.

The blue-uniformed figure **nearest the foreground** is the man on the extreme
right-hand side of the picture: a workman in a bright blue boiler-suit/overalls
and a flat cap, seen from behind, wheeling a bicycle across the paved apron in
front of the small brick building, next to two other bicycles propped against
the wall. His feet are the lowest (and therefore nearest) of any of the blue
figures, so he is the one in question.

## What the train is doing

The locomotive (Southern/BR number **30853**, carrying an "SPL 13" special-train
disc on the smokebox door) is facing the viewer, buffer-beam and buffers towards
us, with its train of vans trailing away behind it to the left. It is clearly
moving **forwards, towards the viewer**: the exhaust is being thrown up and
blown back over the train, and there is a large white cloud of steam low down at
the front from the cylinder drain cocks, which is what you see when a loco is
starting away. So "the same direction" means it continues towards the bottom of
the picture.

It is not coming straight out of the frame, though. The track it is on is on a
sharp curve — you can see the curve echoed by the white-and-red painted kerb of
the traffic island in front of the engine. Tracing the rail that the engine's
leading wheel is actually standing on, it runs from under the wagons on the
left, swings round through the point under the leading wheel, and then runs
**down and to the right across the roadway, leaving the picture through the
bottom edge**, roughly below and to the left of the workman. As the engine runs
forward it therefore moves both towards the viewer and to the right, and off the
bottom-right of the canvas.

## Why he is clear of it

- **He is standing behind the track, not on it.** In the picture his boots are
  noticeably *higher up the canvas* than every rail near him. On a ground plane,
  higher up the canvas means further away from the viewer. All of the rails in
  that part of the picture — including the one that passes closest to him —
  cross the ground *in front of* him, between him and the viewer. There is no
  rail between him and the building behind him.
- **There is a real gap, not a hair's breadth.** Using his own height and his
  bicycle wheel as a scale, his feet are of the order of 3–4 m back from the
  nearest rail of the track immediately in front of him, and roughly 5–6 m from
  the track the locomotive is actually running on. A steam locomotive only
  overhangs its rails by well under a metre, so even at the engine's closest
  approach there are several metres to spare.
- **The geometry is getting better, not worse.** Because the loco's track curves
  away towards the bottom-right corner, the engine is moving *away* from his
  line as well as past him. Its closest approach to him is roughly where it is
  now, or a little further on, and after that it only gets further away.
- **He is off the running surface entirely.** He is on the paved/kerbed apron in
  front of the brick building, the same surface on which the other two bicycles
  are parked against the wall — a pedestrian area, not part of the crossing.

## Caveats worth stating

- He has his **back to the train** and is pushing a bicycle, so he is relying on
  where he is standing rather than on watching the engine. That is exactly why
  "if he stays still" matters: standing still he is fine, but if he were to walk
  a few paces forward (down the picture, towards the viewer) he would step onto
  the crossing and into the danger zone. The answer depends on him not moving
  towards the rails.
- The margin, while adequate, is not enormous by modern safety standards — he is
  within a few metres of a working dockside crossing, and a passing locomotive
  will bring noise, smoke, steam and possibly hot cinders. He would be
  uncomfortable, not injured.
- There appears to be a second, parallel line of rails between him and the
  engine's track. The engine is not on that one, but if it were switched onto it
  the clearance would shrink to roughly two metres — still a miss, but a close
  one. On the route it is visibly set on, this does not arise.

## Conclusion

Yes — the workman in blue overalls with the bicycle, the nearest blue-uniformed
figure to the foreground, is safe if he stays exactly where he is. The
locomotive is running forward on a curve that takes it across the road in front
of him and out of the bottom-right of the picture, passing several metres nearer
to the viewer than he is standing. He is behind all the rails, on the paved area
by the building, and nothing on the train's path reaches him.

## Detailed Technical and Spatial Analysis

### 1. Identification of the Subject and Position
* **The Subject:** The person referred to is the man on the far right of the image. He is wearing a dark blue uniform (matching jacket and trousers with a cap) and is sitting on or leaning against a bicycle.
* **His Location:** He is positioned on a very narrow paved sidewalk on the right side of the image, right in front of the brick building's facade. His bicycle is angled slightly towards the street, and his front wheel is resting right next to the sidewalk curb.

### 2. Train Alignment and Path of Travel
* **The Locomotive:** The train is headed by a massive Southern Railway Lord Nelson class steam locomotive (No. `30853`). 
* **The Direction:** The locomotive is facing forward to the right (as indicated by the front smokebox door, front buffer beam, and the steam/smoke trailing backward over the boiler). 
* **The Track Path:** The train is transitioning from a curved track section on the left onto a straight set of rails embedded in the street pavement (common for dockside and quayside tramways, such as those at the Southampton Docks shown here). These embedded rails run diagonally across the foreground from left to right, passing directly along the curb of the sidewalk where the gentleman is standing, and exiting off-screen at the bottom-right corner.
* **The Trajectory:** If the train continues forward in its current direction, it will travel directly along these rails, passing immediately in front of the brick building and the sidewalk.

### 3. Dimensional Clearance and Overhang (The Hazard)
* **Track Gauge vs. Loading Gauge:** The embedded tracks are standard gauge ($4\text{ ft } 8.5\text{ in}$ or $1.435\text{ m}$). However, a large steam locomotive like the Lord Nelson class has a much wider body (loading gauge), typically measuring around $9\text{ ft}$ ($2.74\text{ m}$) in width. 
* **The Overhang:** Consequently, the locomotive's body, cylinders, cab sides, footsteps, and tender overhang the outer edge of the rails by approximately $1.5\text{ to } 2\text{ feet}$ on each side.

The sidewalk itself is exceptionally narrow—scarcely wider than the length of the bicycle (approximately $3\text{ feet}$ wide) and bounded by a solid brick wall behind the man.
* **The Collision Risk:** Because the locomotive's side overhangs the rails and sweeps across the sidewalk, and because the man is positioned right at the curb with a solid brick wall directly behind him, he has no clearance. If he remains still, he and his bicycle will be directly struck and crushed by the side of the passing locomotive.
